newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: U.N. to sift Rwandan Hutu refugees for soldiers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to sift Rwandan Hutu refugees for soldiers.

text.p: A senior U.N. refugee agency official said on Saturday that it planned to separate former soldiers and militiamen from over 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees scattered throughout Central Africa, mostly in former Zaire.

Assistant High Commissioner for Refugees, Sergio Viera de Mello, said during a two-day working visit to Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo, that those suspected of genocide in Rwanda would be handed over for trial.
"This separation can only happen with the active participation of the governments of the countries concerned," he told reporters in the capital Kinshasa, adding that work could start within a week.
The refugees were among over a million Rwandan Hutus who fled home in 1994 fearing reprisals for the slaughter by Hutu hardliners of hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis in Rwanda.

The agency came under heavy criticism for failing to separate soldiers and Interahamwe militia from the vast civilian refugee population that the hardliners held hostage in camps along the borders with Rwanda and Burundi.
Viera de Mello said the government of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko had failed to respond to repeated appeals from the U.N. refugee agency to weed out the hardliners.

"Congo is no longer Zaire. We hope the new authorities will give us the support that the Zairean government did not give us in '94 and '95," he added. "I think the first teams who will come to assist our colleagues on the ground will be here in a week or 10 days."
Viera de Mello said the agency now expected security, logistical and administrative support from host governments in carrying out the delicate task.

Kabila's own forces, who took up arms against Mobutu in October, have been accused with Rwandan Tutsi allies of massacring Hutu refugees who flooded west after the majority opted to return home in December.

The refugee agency estimates that between 100,000 and 200,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutus are either missing or spread across 10 of the Congo's 11 provinces or in neighbouring Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville.
Kabila has agreed to an international inquiry into massacre allegations.
Vierra de Mello said that as repatriations continued the proportion of former soldiers or militiamen among those refugees remaining was growing.

He said refugees would be vetted during in-depth interviews and those suspected of having participated in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda would be handed over to the international tribunal on the genocide for trial.
The whereabouts of the refugees remains a mystery, many of those in Kabila's Congo are scattered through the jungle in groups of less than 100, the refugee agency says.
The agency has requested that Burundian Hutus be granted asylum until voluntary repatriation there is viable.

Around 20,000 Rwandan refugees reached neighbouring Congo- Brazzaville. President Pascal Lissouba's government, locked in bitter clashes with supporters of his military predecessor, had asked for them to be repatriated by the end of June.
Viera de Mello said access to refugees in Kabila's Congo had improved and government ministers had promised a quick response to queries he raised.
